statement: For how many integers $n$ with $1 \le n \le 1000$ does $\dfrac{n}{1400}$ have a terminating decimal expansion with exactly $3$ digits after the decimal point?

choices.misconception: I required n/7 to be coprime to 10 so that n/1400 stays over the full denominator 200, but n = 35 gives 1/40 = 0.025, which also has three digits.
I subtracted the 7 values with at most one digit after the point from the 142 terminating ones, when I should have subtracted those with at most two digits.
I counted every n that makes the decimal terminate, which means at most three digits after the point, not exactly three.
I thought n only had to be odd, forgetting that the factor 7 in 1400 must cancel for the decimal to terminate at all.

hints: It terminates exactly when $7 \mid n$. Write $n = 7j$, so the fraction is $\dfrac{j}{200}$ with $1 \le j \le 142$.
A decimal has at most $d$ digits after the point exactly when $10^d$ times it is an integer. Compare $1000 \cdot \dfrac{j}{200} = 5j$ with $100 \cdot \dfrac{j}{200} = \dfrac{j}{2}$.

solutions.reliable: Since $1400 = 2^3 \cdot 5^2 \cdot 7$, the fraction $n/1400$ in lowest terms has a denominator free of primes other than $2$ and $5$ exactly when the $7$ cancels, that is, when $7 \mid n$. Write $n = 7j$ with $1 \le j \le 142$; the fraction is $j/200$. A terminating decimal has at most $d$ digits after the point exactly when $10^d$ times it is an integer. Here $1000 \cdot j/200 = 5j$ is always an integer, so every such decimal has at most $3$ digits, and $100 \cdot j/200 = j/2$ is an integer exactly when $j$ is even. So there are exactly $3$ digits when $j$ is odd. The odd $j$ from $1$ to $142$ number $71$, so the answer is $71$. For example, $n = 7$ gives $0.005$ and $n = 35$ gives $0.025$.
solutions.elegant: In lowest terms $j/200 = j/(2^3 \cdot 5^2)$ becomes $a/(2^m 5^k)$, which has $\max(m, k)$ digits after the point. Since $k \le 2$, the count is $3$ exactly when $m = 3$, that is, when $j$ is odd. There are $71$ odd $j$ in $1, \ldots, 142$.
